overview:
Maitri‑bhavana (Skt. *maitrī-bhāvanā*, Prakrit *mettī-bhāvaṇā*) is a foundational contemplative practice in Jainism centered on cultivating universal friendliness, goodwill, and non‑harm toward all living beings. It appears across Śvetāmbara and Digambara traditions as one of the core *bhāvanās*—structured reflections that support ethical conduct, reduce passions (*kaṣāyas*), and prepare the mind for right perception (*samyak‑darśana*). In classical sources, maitri is not merely an emotion but a disciplined mental orientation that counters anger, hostility, and aversion. It is closely linked to *ahiṃsā*, because genuine non‑violence requires an inner disposition of benevolence toward all forms of life.

In early canonical contexts, maitri is described as a state of wishing well-being for all souls, regardless of their current condition or relationship to oneself. Later commentarial traditions expand this into a meditative exercise: the practitioner intentionally generates thoughts of friendliness toward teachers, peers, adversaries, and even beings unknown to them. This practice is said to soften karmic inflows (*āsrava*) by weakening the passions that bind karma, especially anger and pride.

Modern Jain communities often teach maitri‑bhavana as one of the four *bhāvanās* used in daily reflection (maitri, pramoda, karuṇā, and madhyastha). It is presented as a practical tool for laypeople to cultivate emotional stability, reduce interpersonal conflict, and deepen empathy. While the form varies—recitation, silent contemplation, or structured meditation—the underlying aim remains consistent: to establish a mental field of friendliness that supports ethical living and spiritual progress.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.translation: Friendliness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11 lists the four attitudes (*bhāvanās*) that support right conduct. Commentaries (e.g., Pūjyapāda’s *Sarvārthasiddhi*) explain maitri as goodwill toward those who are virtuous, reducing envy and hostility.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: One should cultivate the feeling of friendliness.
primary_sources.notes: Appears in didactic sections encouraging the aspirant to develop inner dispositions that weaken passions. Editions vary; phrasing may differ slightly across manuscripts.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka Niryukti (referenced tradition)
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabāhu (traditional attribution)
primary_sources.translation: One should enter into the contemplation of friendliness.
primary_sources.notes: The *Āvaśyaka* literature elaborates the six obligatory duties, including contemplations. Maitri is framed as a mental purification practice. Exact wording varies across recensions; quoted lines represent attested forms but may differ in manuscripts.

misconceptions.myth: Maitri‑bhavana is only about feeling affection toward people one already likes.
misconceptions.reality: Classical Jain texts emphasize maitri toward all beings, including adversaries and strangers. It is a disciplined practice meant to counter anger and hostility, not a selective emotional preference.

misconceptions.myth: Maitri‑bhavana is a modern, non-traditional meditation borrowed from other religions.
misconceptions.reality: Maitri appears in early Jain canonical and commentarial literature. While modern presentations may resemble contemporary mindfulness practices, the concept and terminology are authentically Jain and historically attested.

misconceptions.myth: Maitri‑bhavana alone can remove karmic bondage.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine states that maitri supports the reduction of passions, which in turn reduces karmic inflow. It is one component of a broader path involving right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.
